content: This report consolidates and summarizes all recommendations from the CDC's Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) regarding the prevention and control of tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis in the United States. It serves as a comprehensive resource for clinicians and public health providers, replacing all previously published reports and policy notes. No new recommendations are included in this document. The ACIP recommends routine vaccination against tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis. Infants and young children should receive a 5-dose series of the diphtheria and tetanus toxoids and acellular pertussis (DTaP) vaccine, followed by a single adolescent booster dose of the tetanus toxoid, reduced diphtheria toxoid, and acellular pertussis (Tdap) vaccine. Adults who have not previously received Tdap are also advised to receive a booster dose. Pregnant women are recommended to receive a dose of Tdap during each pregnancy, ideally between 27 and 36 weeks of gestation, regardless of prior Tdap vaccination history. The ACIP develops recommendations for the routine use of vaccines in children, adolescents, and adults. These recommendations are harmonized with those of other professional organizations, including the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), the American Academy of Family Physicians (AAFP), and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG). Recommendations for adults are also aligned with the AAFP, ACOG, and the American College of Physicians (ACP). Once approved by the CDC Director, ACIP recommendations become official agency guidelines upon publication in the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report (MMWR). Historically, vaccination against pertussis, diphtheria, and tetanus began in the late 1940s with the use of the combined diphtheria and tetanus toxoids and whole-cell pertussis (DTP) vaccine. Due to safety concerns associated with the whole-cell pertussis component, DTaP vaccines were developed and replaced DTP in the 1990s. Since 1997, infants and young children have been recommended to receive a 5-dose series of DTaP. In 2005, ACIP recommended a single dose of Tdap for adolescents and adults, with subsequent booster doses of tetanus and diphtheria toxoids (Td) every 10 years or as indicated for wound management. In 2012, to reduce the burden of pertussis in infants, ACIP recommended Tdap vaccination during each pregnancy. Pertussis is an acute respiratory disease caused by Bordetella pertussis. It progresses through three phases: catarrhal (characterized by mild cough, coryza, and low-grade fever), paroxysmal (marked by spasmodic cough, post-tussive vomiting, and inspiratory whoop), and convalescent (gradual symptom resolution over weeks to months). Factors influencing clinical presentation include age, immunity level, vaccination history, and early antimicrobial use. Pertussis is primarily transmitted via respiratory droplets and is most infectious during the catarrhal and early paroxysmal phases. Antibiotics such as azithromycin, clarithromycin, erythromycin, or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole are used to treat pertussis and prevent its spread. Tetanus is a life-threatening but vaccine-preventable disease caused by the neurotoxin Clostridium tetani. The bacterium's spores enter the body through skin or mucosal breaches, germinate under anaerobic conditions, and produce tetanospasmin, a potent exotoxin that causes muscle spasms and rigidity. The disease is not transmitted person-to-person. The incubation period ranges from 3 to 21 days, with shorter periods associated with more severe disease. Without high-quality medical care, the case-fatality ratio can reach 100%, though it is approximately 10%-20% in modern healthcare settings. Tetanus primarily affects older adults, reflecting waning immunity or lack of primary vaccination. Diphtheria is an acute, communicable illness caused by toxigenic strains of Corynebacterium diphtheriae. Respiratory diphtheria is characterized by a gray pseudomembrane in the nasopharynx, tonsils, or larynx, which can extend into the trachea-bronchial tree, causing airway obstruction. Systemic absorption of diphtheria toxin can lead to cardiac and neurologic complications. Diphtheria cases in the U.S. have declined dramatically since the introduction of universal childhood vaccination in the 1940s, with only sporadic cases reported in recent decades. Immunity wanes without decennial booster doses, leaving older adults potentially unprotected. The ACIP emphasizes the importance of completing the 5-dose childhood DTaP series before age 7, followed by adolescent and decennial adult boosters with Td or Tdap to maintain immunity against tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis. Vaccination coverage varies across age groups, with high rates among children but lower rates among older adults. Continued surveillance and vaccination efforts are critical to controlling these vaccine-preventable diseases.
